citing_sentences: As shown in Fig. 1 (top), interactive loop in InteractiveWorld consists of three components: (1) an Assistant agent that, like a real wearable assistant, shares the human’s egocentric view, receives the task from the human, and decides when and how to offer natural-language guidance; (2) a Human agent, driven by an MLLM, that interprets the guidance based on its observations and converts it into high-level commands from 36 action primitives (e.g., [Grab]<cup>), much as a person translates advice into behavior; and (3) an Interactive Environment that stably executes these commands through a full-body human model capable of autonomous navigation, posture adaptation, and collision-free manipulation, while continuously rendering the resulting first-person view.

abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user’s physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today’s MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

sections.body: The paper argues that existing egocentric benchmarks are static: a model answers questions about a fixed recording, and the video does not change with its answers. It introduces InteractiveWorld, built on Isaac Sim with over 8,000 objects and 50 scenes. In it, an Assistant agent gives natural-language guidance to a Human agent, which acts through 36 action primitives, and the environment updates what the human sees next. The paper also introduces InteractiveBench, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories, scored by verifiable final object states. The authors state that real-world experiments are costly and hard to scale.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Static video benchmarks cannot test whether interactive assistants help people, so the paper proposes a closed-loop simulated environment and benchmark.

sections.body: The environment has three layers. The Physical Layer uses an SMPL+H body driven kinematically, with a head camera and collision checks against a proxy rig of 17 capsules and a head sphere. The Human Action Layer plans walking paths with `A*` search and adapts posture and arm trajectories to each target object. The Semantic Layer maps commands that name an action and a target, such as a Grab command for a cup, to these actions. After each action, the simulator updates object states and renders a new first-person view. The paper states that the body is deliberately kinematic rather than a ragdoll, and that unsafe actions are rejected with a failure reason returned to the upper layer.
sections.heading: InteractiveWorld
sections.headline: InteractiveWorld models a human who follows assistant guidance, using kinematic body control, collision checks and 36 action primitives.

sections.body: The benchmark contains 120 tasks across Guidance, Planning, Accessibility, Decision, Prevention and Finding. Each task defines a starting scene, a warmup stage, and a closed-loop interaction in which the assistant chooses to stay silent, guide, or end the task. Termination occurs when the assistant outputs done or reaches a maximum interaction limit. A task succeeds only if all predefined core states hold at the end. The authors report that an Oracle Assistant gives a 100% pass rate with the same Human agent, and no assistance gives 0%. Visual inputs are withheld from the human in Accessibility tasks.
sections.heading: InteractiveBench
sections.headline: InteractiveBench has 120 human-reviewed tasks in six categories, scored by final simulator object states rather than answer matching.

sections.body: Twelve frontier MLLMs were tested as the Assistant, with Gemini 3.1 Pro as the Human agent. Claude Fable 5.1 has the highest average pass rate at 41.7%, and every other model is at or below 33.3%. The best Decision pass rate is 85.0%. The authors attribute the Guidance and Planning gap to tasks requiring continuous tracking and replanning. Across models, visual perception and memory errors account for 70.4% to 85.7% of first errors. Models also show action redundancy, with the efficiency analysis reporting 2.35 to 3.66 times the Oracle's cost on Accessibility and Guidance. The Human agent is a model, not a real person.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: The strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, passes 41.7% of tasks, and the best models reach only 20.0% on Guidance and 25.0% on Planning.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the two contributions. InteractiveWorld is a verifiable environment for closed-loop human-assistant interaction. InteractiveBench is a dynamic benchmark of 120 multi-turn tasks. The authors state that InteractiveWorld measures interactive abilities with verifiable rewards, and that InteractiveBench evaluates how models assist people in the real world. They present both as a foundation for developing and evaluating interactive MLLMs. The section does not report new experimental results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: InteractiveWorld and InteractiveBench provide a verifiable foundation for developing and evaluating interactive MLLM assistants.

sections.body: Appendix A compares egocentric assistant benchmarks, assistant models, and robot-centric and interaction-oriented simulators. Appendix B gives implementation details for the physical, human action and semantic layers, including the SMPL+H model and collision handling. Appendix C describes benchmark construction, evaluation protocol, metrics and the task catalog. Appendix D reports error-type settings, memory augmentation, a static versus dynamic comparison, task horizon results, and a comparison of model-based and real human executors on 36 tasks. Appendix E lists planned future work, including a reinforcement learning platform and more realistic scenes.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, simulator implementation, benchmark construction and metrics, extra analyses, human-executor validation and future work.
